text: Novartis AG v. Union of India (2013) — Supreme Court landmark on Section 3(d). Facts: Novartis sought patent for Gleevec (imatinib mesylate beta crystalline form) — a new form of known compound. Issue: Does Section 3(d) require 'enhanced efficacy' for new forms? Held: Patent denied. 'Efficacy' in Section 3(d) means therapeutic efficacy for pharmaceutical patents. New form must show significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy, not just better physical properties (solubility, bioavailability). Novartis failed to show therapeutic improvement. Impact for AYUSH: new forms of known herbs need clinical efficacy data, not just better absorption.

Bayer Corporation v. Natco Pharma (2012) — First compulsory license in India. Facts: Natco applied for compulsory license on Bayer's Sorafenib (cancer drug). Bayer's price: Rs 2.8 lakh/month. Arguments: drug not available at affordable price, not worked in India. Held: Compulsory license granted. Royalty: 6% of net sales to Bayer. Natco price: Rs 8,800/month. Impact: Established that high pricing and non-working trigger compulsory licensing. For AYUSH: price patented products reasonably, manufacture in India to avoid compulsory license risk.

Turmeric Patent Case (1997) — USPTO revocation of biopiracy patent. Facts: University of Mississippi Medical Center received US patent on turmeric's wound healing properties (traditional use). India's CSIR challenged patent with prior art from Sanskrit texts. Outcome: USPTO revoked patent for lack of novelty — prior art in traditional knowledge. Significance: Established that traditional knowledge can be prior art even against patents in other countries. Led to TKDL creation. For AYUSH: demonstrates importance of prior art documentation and international challenge capability.

Neem Patent Case (2005) — EPO revocation. Facts: W.R. Grace and USDA obtained European patent on neem-based fungicide formulation. India's government and NGOs challenged, arguing traditional knowledge. Outcome: EPO revoked patent after 10-year battle — prior art in Indian traditional agricultural practices. Significance: Major biopiracy case supporting traditional knowledge as prior art. Contributed to global awareness. For AYUSH: validate that traditional use can invalidate patents worldwide; document and defend against biopiracy.

Basmati Rice Case (2001) — RiceTec patent challenge. Facts: US company RiceTec obtained US patent on 'Basmati' rice lines and name. India challenged — Basmati is Indian geographical indication. Outcome: RiceTec narrowed claims, withdrew 'Basmati' name claims. India strengthened GI protection for Basmati. Significance: Highlighted need for GI protection, traditional variety documentation. For AYUSH: protect geographically specific products through GI registration, not just patents.

Section 3(p) Traditional Knowledge Cases: Multiple patent applications rejected at Indian Patent Office for being traditional knowledge. Examples: Giloy (Tinospora cordifolia) formulations described in classical texts, Triphala combinations matching Ayurvedic prescriptions, Ashwagandha compositions found in TKDL. Process: Examiner cites TKDL references, applicant must distinguish or abandon. For AYUSH: proactive TKDL searching before filing prevents wasteful applications; differentiate through novel processing, ratios, delivery systems.

Merck Sharp Dohme v. Glenmark Generics (2015) — Patent term and interim injunction. Facts: Merck sought injunction against Glenmark's generic version of Sitagliptin (diabetes drug). Issue: Balance of convenience, public interest in affordable medicines. Held: Interim injunction granted but with condition that Glenmark can continue if they deposit royalty. Impact: Courts balance patentee rights with public access. For AYUSH: in seeking injunctions, consider public health implications; courts weigh access to medicines.

F. Hoffmann-La Roche v. Cipla (2008-2012) — Erlotinib (cancer drug) case. Facts: Roche sought interim injunction against Cipla's generic Erlotinib. Roche price: Rs 4,800/tablet. Cipla price: Rs 1,600. Issue: Balance of convenience, public interest. Held: Interim injunction DENIED — public interest in affordable cancer drugs outweighs patentee's interest. Significance: Indian courts consider price and access to essential medicines. For AYUSH: patented medicines for serious conditions face similar public interest arguments.

John Richard Brady v. Chemical Process Equipments (1987) — Trade secret injunction. Facts: Employee left company and used trade secrets (manufacturing know-how) at new employer. Held: Injunction granted restraining use of confidential information. Significance: Established trade secret protection through contract and equity in India. For AYUSH: employment agreements with confidentiality clauses are enforceable; protect formulation know-how through contracts.

Monsanto Technology v. Nuziveedu Seeds (2019) — Plant variety and patent interface. Facts: Dispute over Bt cotton technology licensing and patent coverage. Issue: Whether Section 3(j) (plants not patentable) applies to genetically modified traits. Held: Complex proceedings; parties settled. Highlighted tension between Patents Act and PPVFR Act. Impact: Uncertainty on biotechnology patents for plants. For AYUSH: genetic modification of medicinal plants faces similar legal questions.

Bristol-Myers Squibb v. J.D. Joshi (2015) — Section 3(d) interpretation. Facts: Patent application for crystalline form of Atazanavir. Issue: Whether stability improvement qualifies as enhanced efficacy under Section 3(d). Held: Stability alone not sufficient — must show therapeutic efficacy enhancement. Impact: Reinforced Novartis interpretation that efficacy means therapeutic efficacy. For AYUSH: stability improvements alone don't overcome Section 3(d); need clinical efficacy data.

Bajaj Auto Ltd. v. TVS Motor Company (2009) — Patent infringement interim relief. Facts: Bajaj alleged TVS's Flame motorcycle infringed patent on DTSi technology. Sought interim injunction. Held: Prima facie case established; interim injunction granted considering Bajaj's investment in R&D and marketing. Significance: Demonstrated courts will grant interim relief for patent infringement. For AYUSH: valuable patents can be enforced through interim injunctions.

Natco Pharma v. BDR Pharmaceuticals (2020) — Pre-grant opposition. Facts: Natco filed pre-grant opposition against BDR's formulation patent. Grounds: Prior art, Section 3(d), obviousness. Outcome: Opposition successful; patent application rejected. Significance: Pre-grant opposition is effective tool against weak patents. For AYUSH: monitor competitor filings, oppose where appropriate; build strong applications to withstand opposition.

AstraZeneca AB v. Intas Pharma (2020) — Patent damages. Facts: After successful infringement suit, AstraZeneca sought damages for lost profits. Issue: Calculation of damages for pharmaceutical patent infringement. Held: Damages awarded based on reasonable royalty approach. Significance: Guidance on damages calculation in pharma patent cases. For AYUSH: maintain sales records to support damages claims in infringement suits.

Ericsson v. Xiaomi (2014-15) — SEP and FRAND licensing. Facts: Ericsson alleged Xiaomi infringed standard-essential patents. Issue: Obligation to license on FRAND terms. Held: Interim injunction granted but stayed by Supreme Court pending FRAND negotiation. Significance: Balance between patent rights and fair licensing for essential technology. For AYUSH: less directly relevant but shows courts balance interests in IP enforcement.
